title: STAPO: Selective Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agent Training

paper.title: STAPO: Selective Trajectory-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agent Training
paper.abstract:
Abstract Reinforcement Learning (RL) is the dominant paradigm for training Large Language Model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. However, sparse and delayed rewards often lead to trajectory neglect , in which agents lose focus on the task goal and interaction history at intermediate steps.
Prior work has explored step-level supervision using Shannon-entropy–based uncertainty signals, which conflate inherent state complexity with agent confidence and therefore provide unreliable estimates of decision reliability. To address this issue, we propose normalized entropy , which measures confidence deviations relative to an agent’s average behavior under a given state, thereby strengthening the association between low-quality actions and trajectory neglect.
Building on this insight, we introduce S elective T rajectory- A ware P olicy O ptimization (STAPO), a hierarchical group-based RL framework. STAPO leverages normalized entropy to locate outlier steps associated with trajectory neglect and optimizes them via a joint mechanism of trajectory-aware reward and trajectory-independent penalty , enhancing trajectory awareness while preserving training stability.
Extensive experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-Augmented QA demonstrate that STAPO achieves state-of-the-art performance while substantially alleviating trajectory neglect, validating its effectiveness and robustness for agentic tasks.

Affiliation: Zhejiang University Abstract Reinforcement Learning (RL) is the dominant paradigm for training Large Language Model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. However, sparse and delayed rewards often lead to trajectory neglect , in which agents lose focus on the task goal and interaction history at intermediate steps. Prior work has explored step-level supervision using Shannon-entropy–based uncertainty signals, which conflate inherent state complexity with agent confidence and therefore provide unreliable estimates of decision reliability. To address this issue, we propose normalized entropy , which measures confidence deviations relative to an agent’s average behavior under a given state, thereby strengthening the association between low-quality actions and trajectory neglect. Building on this insight, we introduce S elective T rajectory- A ware P olicy O ptimization (STAPO), a hierarchical group-based RL framework. STAPO leverages normalized entropy to locate outlier steps associated with trajectory neglect and optimizes them via a joint mechanism of trajectory-aware reward and trajectory-independent penalty , enhancing trajectory awareness while preserving training stability. Extensive experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-Augmented QA demonstrate that STAPO achieves state-of-the-art performance while substantially alleviating trajectory neglect, validating its effectiveness and robustness for agentic tasks. Figure 1: Illustration of the differences between Shannon entropy and normalized entropy in locating trajectory neglect. 1 Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) have evolved from static text generators to autonomous agents capable of executing complex, long-horizon tasks, such as embodied control ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ; Li et al., 2024 ) and web navigation ( Furuta et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ; Gou et al., 2025 ) . To enable long-horizon reasoning in LLM agents, recent work has increasingly adopted Reinforcement Learning (RL) for post-training. In particular, group-based RL algorithms such as RLOO ( Kool et al., 2019 ; Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) and GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) estimate advantages via group sampling, avoiding explicit critic training while improving scalability and training stability. However, training agents for long-horizon tasks remains challenging due to the temporal credit assignment problem induced by sparse and delayed rewards. As illustrated in Figure 1 , agents often exhibit trajectory neglect , where the model loses focus on the task goal and interaction history during extended interaction sequences, leading to low-quality actions at certain intermediate steps (see Appendix A for detailed case studies). While recent adaptations like GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) and RLVMR ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) attempt to mitigate the credit assignment issue by achieving fine-grained step-level advantage estimation, they typically optimize all steps indiscriminately, lacking a selective mechanism to precisely locate and address these outlier steps caused by trajectory neglect. Furthermore, several works have explored leveraging internal uncertainty signals to assist training, including entropy-based regularization and supervision strategies ( Xu et al., 2025 ; Cui et al., 2025 ) . However, these approaches predominantly rely on Shannon entropy computed from step-level action distributions, which conflates inherent state complexity with agent confidence. As shown in Figure 1 , a high-entropy step may simply reflect a genuinely complex state with numerous plausible actions, rather than a lack of confidence. Consequently, raw Shannon entropy provides an unreliable signal for locating outlier steps associated with trajectory neglect (as empirically illustrated in Appendix B ). To address these limitations, we first propose a novel metric: normalized entropy . By aggregating actions from the same state across sampled trajectories, normalized entropy measures uncertainty relative to the state average, effectively decoupling inherent state complexity from model confidence. Our empirical analysis shows that outliers located by normalized entropy consistently correlate with trajectory neglect, which we empirically find to be strongly associated with low-quality actions. Building on this insight, we introduce S elective T rajectory- A ware P olicy O ptimization (STAPO), a hierarchical group-based RL framework. STAPO operates in two phases: (1) Outlier Localization , which dynamically locates outlier steps using normalized entropy statistics; and (2) Selective Optimization , which targets these steps associated with trajectory neglect. Specifically, STAPO incorporates a trajectory-aware reward to encourage stronger focus on trajectories, balanced by a trajectory-independent penalty to mitigate the risk of reward hacking. Extensive experiments on representative agentic benchmarks, including ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ) , WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) , and Search-Augmented QA, demonstrate that STAPO consistently outperforms strong baselines such as GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) and EMPG ( Wang et al., 2025a ) , while attribution analysis further confirms its effectiveness in alleviating trajectory neglect. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose normalized entropy to decouple state complexity from agent confidence and effectively locate low-quality actions and trajectory neglect. • We introduce STAPO , a hierarchical group-based RL framework that integrates outlier localization with a joint optimization mechanism of trajectory-aware reward and trajectory-independent penalty. • Extensive experiments demonstrate that STAPO achieves superior performance and robustness across diverse agentic tasks, while substantially mitigating trajectory neglect. 2 Related Work 2.1 LLM Agents Large Language Models (LLMs) have increasingly been developed into autonomous agents capable of perceiving, reasoning, and acting in dynamic environments ( Zhang and Zhang, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024a ; Zitkovich et al., 2023 ) . Early approaches primarily relied on prompt-based methods, such as ReAct ( Yao et al., 2023 ) and Reflexion ( Shinn et al., 2024 ) , as well as enhanced memory, retrieval mechanisms ( Wang et al., 2024b ; Tan et al., 2024 ) , and integration with external tools ( Schick et al., 2023 ; Xie et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) . More recent work has shifted toward adapting model parameters through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) ( Zhang and Zhang, 2024 ) or reinforcement learning (RL) ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ) , enabling agents to learn directly from environment interactions. 2.2 Group-based Policy Optimization To avoid the high overhead and instability associated with training independent critic models, group-based RL methods have emerged as promising alternatives to traditional actor-critic methods (like PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) ). These algorithms, such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , RLOO ( Kool et al., 2019 ; Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) , and DAPO ( Yu et al., 2025 ) leverage a group of samples from the same query and estimate the advantages accordingly. Recently, GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) , RLVMR ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , and Tree-GRPO ( Ji et al., 2025 ) further advance this paradigm by introducing hierarchical grouping structures to achieve fine-grained step-level advantage estimation without relying on auxiliary models. However, they optimize all steps indiscriminately, lacking a selective mechanism to precisely locate and address outlier steps caused by trajectory neglect. 2.3 Entropy-based Reinforcement Learning To overcome the challenges of sparse external rewards, recent works have explored using internal feedback (like model uncertainty, frequently quantified by entropy) to assist training ( Agarwal et al., 2025 ) . However, most of them rely on raw Shannon entropy, which conflates inherent state complexity with agent confidence, and primarily utilize it as a proxy for regularization or re-weighting. For instance, EPO ( Xu et al., 2025 ) stabilizes exploration via entropy smoothing regularization; EMPG ( Wang et al., 2025a ) modulates the advantage term using entropy weights; and Cui et al. (2025) leverages entropy to truncate gradients for specific tokens. In contrast, we propose normalized entropy to decouple inherent state complexity from agent confidence, employing it to precisely locate outlier steps for selective trajectory-aware optimization. 3 Empirical Analysis In this section, we formalize the task definitions, detail our statistical strategy for outlier localization based on a novel normalized entropy metric, and empirically validate its effectiveness in locating low-quality actions and trajectory neglect. 3.1 Task Definitions Formally, we consider a general setting where an LLM agent interacts with an environment in discrete time steps t = 1 , 2 , … , T t=1,2,\dots,T . The initial input instruction x x consists of a system prompt p p (defining general rules and roles) and a specific task goal g g . At each step t t , the agent receives a current observation s t s_{t} and maintains an interaction history h t = ( s 1 , a 1 , … , s t − 1 , a t − 1 ) h_{t}=(s_{1},a_{1},\dots,s_{t-1},a_{t-1}) . The complete prompt at step t t is denoted as c t = ( p , g , h t , s t ) c_{t}=(p,g,h_{t},s_{t}) , conditioned on which the model policy π θ \pi_{\theta} generates an action a t a_{t} . To analyze agent behavior, we sample a group of N N full trajectories { τ 1 , τ 2 , … , τ N } \{\tau_{1},\tau_{2},\dots,\tau_{N}\} for each instruction x x . We define an anchor state s ~ \tilde{s} as the canonical state identity used for grouping semantically equivalent step contexts within the current batch (exact-match keys for structured observations and similarity-based keys for free-text observations). Within a single training epoch, each sampled step is assigned to exactly one anchor state via hard clustering (exact match or greedy maximum-similarity assignment), so no step simultaneously belongs to multiple groups. We then utilize the anchor state grouping mechanism ( Feng et al., 2025 ) to aggregate actions from the same state across sampled trajectories.
